idiom_name: the ? operator over Result<T, E> (Try/From-based propagation)
implementation_notes: Result and Option are the standard monads: Ok/Some is unit, and_then is bind for explicit chains, and ? is the desugared bind - it yields Ok's value or early-returns Err, converting the error through From so one function can mix error types. The work happens in the compiler rather than behind a trait object and Option<T> over a pointer stays pointer-sized via the null-pointer optimization, so there is no monadic overhead to pay. Use combinator chains when the pipeline must stay a value; use ? in ordinary functions.
pitfalls: ? requires the enclosing function to return a compatible effect (or a type convertible through From); inside a closure returning another type it does not compile.
and_then chains only the same effect: mixing Option and Result needs ok_or/ok_or_else or transpose, with no automatic conversion.
Because ? is an early return, code placed after it may never run; rely on Drop/guards for cleanup instead of hand-written release.

variants.name: map + and_then combinator chains
variants.implementation_notes: The value-level form chains and_then (bind) and map (map) explicitly, which keeps the effect visible and works anywhere - including inside closures and adapter code where ? is unavailable because the closure's return type differs. Prefer it for short chains and stored step functions; switch to ? once the chain grows or mixed error types need From conversions.
pitfalls: Nested and_then pyramids appear quickly; the ? operator exists precisely to linearise them.
and_then cannot mix Option and Result, so heterogeneous chains need ok_or/transpose hops that obscure the flow.

variants.name: async fn + .await over Future
variants.idiom_name: async fn + .await (Future as the IO monad)
variants.implementation_notes: Future is the IO monad, async fn is unit and .await is bind: it suspends the task until the future resolves and yields the value, while a runtime (Tokio, async-std) drives execution. Because futures are inert until polled, nothing happens until the chain is awaited or spawned - the description/interpretation split is explicit in the language - and failures ride inside the future's Output like any other value.
pitfalls: Futures do nothing until polled: building one and dropping it silently cancels the work.
Async blocks capture references across await points, so borrows must outlive the future; use owned data or scoped tasks when spawning.
A runtime must be chosen and its flavour respected: blocking inside an async context (std::thread::sleep, blocking I/O) stalls the executor's worker threads.
